subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before a booking is made.
summary: The brand work here is confident and the site is clean. “Book Now” is a real booking action in a solid, high-contrast button, and the hero video shows the practice's own treatment room and signage rather than stock photography. A visitor can see this is a real place.

What they cannot see is what happens in it. The headline reads “This is Miami Elegance” — the practice's own name, which everyone arriving already knew. No treatment is named on the first screen, no practitioner or credential appears, no review or rating is shown, and there is no telephone number. A patient searching for injectables cannot tell from this screen whether the practice offers them.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the homepage on desktop and mobile plus publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed, so the score is normalised across the six categories that were. Nothing here uses private analytics, and no traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Treatment content and technical performance were not reviewed and are excluded rather than guessed. The presentation is strong; what is missing is the information a patient needs in order to act on it.

scorecard.finding: The headline is the practice's own name and nothing else.
No practitioner, credential or review before the decision.
A strong Book Now button; no phone number anywhere on the first screen.
One clear action, with nothing supporting it.
Clean and legible; an autoplaying video and no tap-to-call.
Miami is in the name; no address appears on the first screen.

strengthsLead: The foundations are good. Almost everything below is about adding information rather than changing what is there.

strengths.title: “Book Now” is a real booking action.
strengths.body: Solid black, high contrast, unmistakably a button, and it asks for the appointment rather than inviting a browse. Many practices put “Our Services” in that position and lose the visitor who had already decided.

strengths.title: The hero shows the actual practice.
strengths.body: The video is the practice's own treatment room and neon signage, not a stock model. Real premises build more confidence than a photograph a patient may have seen on three other sites.

strengths.title: One action, no competition.
strengths.body: A single call to action on the first screen. No banner, no pop-up, no second button pulling attention away — which is rarer than it should be.

strengths.title: The brand presentation is genuinely elegant.
strengths.body: Typography, colour and restraint are all handled well. For a practice selling aesthetic judgement, a site that demonstrates taste is doing real work.

captionDesktop: Desktop, 1366×768. The hero video plays the treatment room, with the headline and a single Book Now button over it.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. “This is Miami Elegance” and “Book Now”. No treatment named, no phone number, no proof of any kind on this screen.

findings.heading: The headline is the name of the practice.
findings.evidence: The hero reads “THIS IS MIAMI ELEGANCE”, in the largest text on the page, with the practice's logo directly above it.
findings.why: Everyone reading it arrived by clicking that name, so it adds nothing. The most valuable space on the site is spent confirming something the visitor already knew, in place of what the practice does and who it is for.
findings.recommended: Let the logo carry the name and give the headline the offer. Naming the treatments a patient came looking for — and Miami — would do more in one line than the brand statement does in three words.

findings.heading: No treatment is named on the first screen.
findings.evidence: The opening screen carries the logo, the headline, the Book Now button and the video. No treatment, category or clinical service appears anywhere on it.
findings.why: A patient searching for lip filler, or laser, or skin tightening cannot tell whether this practice offers it. They have to press Book Now on faith, or leave — and most will do the second. Search engines face the same problem for the same reason.
findings.recommended: Add a single line beneath the headline naming the main treatment categories. It costs nothing visually and answers the question that decides whether the visitor stays.

findings.heading: Nothing on the first screen suggests who performs the treatment.
findings.evidence: No practitioner is named, no qualification, licence or supervising physician is stated, and no patient review or rating appears on the first screen.
findings.why: For injectables the deciding question is who is holding the needle. An elegant room answers a different question — comfort — and leaves the clinical one open. A patient who cannot resolve it here resolves it at a practice that says so plainly.
findings.recommended: Name the treating practitioner with qualification and a real photograph, and place a rating with its review count beside the Book Now button.

findings.heading: There is no phone number on the first screen.
findings.evidence: No telephone number appears in the header or hero on either desktop or mobile.
findings.why: Booking online suits the decided patient. The undecided one — who has a question about suitability, or price, or downtime — has no way to ask, and a proportion of those would have converted on a two-minute call.
findings.recommended: Add a tap-to-call number beside the Book Now button on mobile and in the header on desktop. It costs one line and captures the patient who wants to speak before committing.

findings.heading: The video plays automatically, with a pause control over it.
findings.evidence: The hero is an autoplaying video with a pause button visible in the lower right of the frame on mobile.
findings.why: Autoplaying video consumes mobile data before a visitor has decided the site is worth it, and on a slower connection the first thing they see may be a blank frame. The exposed pause control also signals “player” rather than “background”, which reads less polished than the brand work deserves.
findings.recommended: Keep the footage — it is genuinely good — but consider a still frame as the first thing painted, with the video loading behind it, and hide the player controls.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: Layout follows convention cleanly — logo, menu, hero, single action. Nothing confuses.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: The Book Now button is a good size and well positioned for a thumb.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: There is no proof anywhere on the first screen to place near anything.
No clinician, credential or qualification appears before the booking action.
Strong. A single action, presented without competition — this part is done properly.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: None available: with no treatments listed, the visitor has nothing to choose between yet.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: Showing the real room rather than a stock model is a genuine credibility asset and works in the practice's favour.

roadmap.actions: Replace the headline with the offer and name the main treatment categories beneath it. Add a tap-to-call number beside Book Now. Hide the video player controls.
Name the treating practitioner with qualification and photograph. Add a rating and review count beside the booking button. Put the address on the first screen.
Treatment-page depth with realistic expectations. Post-treatment review requests to build a public rating. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above become yours.

limitations: Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available).
